topic: Christianity / Islam / Judaism / Buddhism / Hinduism / Sikhism: Social & Historical Developments
subject: religious-studies

items.title: Caste is a complex social hierarchy with religious framings
items.claim: How does the caste system relate to Hindu religion?

options.text: It is purely social with no religious dimension

Varna (the fourfold theoretical division — Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras) is described in the Vedas and the Manusmriti; jati (thousands of birth-based occupational groupings) is the lived reality; modern reform movements (Ambedkar, Gandhi, contemporary Dalit activism) have contested its religious basis
Caste was invented by British colonisers

items.reveal:
The Rig Veda's Purusha Sukta (10.90) describes the four varnas emerging from a cosmic being. The Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE-200 CE) codifies caste duties.

Dalits (formerly 'untouchables') were treated as outside the varna system. B.R. Ambedkar (1891-1956), Dalit leader and chief architect of India's constitution, converted to Buddhism in 1956 partly to escape caste. The Indian Constitution (1950) outlaws untouchability.

The relationship between varna theory and the thousands of jatis on the ground is complex. Caste discrimination persists in many forms — the UK Equality Act 2010 includes caste under race discrimination provisions.
items.why: Religious texts and social systems interact in ways that resist clean separation. The caste case shows how a religious tradition can be deployed for social hierarchy and also generate its own critics.

items.title: Varna (theory) and jati (lived caste) are not identical
items.claim: What is the relationship between varna and jati?

options.text: Varna is the fourfold theoretical division (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) described in the Vedas and Manusmriti; jati is the thousands of birth-based occupational groupings that form the lived caste system; Dalits ('untouchables') were outside the four varnas
Caste is purely social with no religious dimension
Caste was invented by British colonisers

items.reveal:
The Rig Veda's Purusha Sukta (10.90) describes the four varnas emerging from a cosmic being. The Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE-200 CE) codifies caste duties.

B. R. Ambedkar (1891-1956), Dalit leader and chief architect of India's constitution, converted to Buddhism in 1956 with around 500,000 followers, partly to escape caste. The Indian Constitution (1950) outlaws untouchability.

The relationship between varna theory and the thousands of jatis on the ground is complex and historically contested. Caste discrimination persists in many forms; the UK Equality Act 2010 includes caste under race discrimination provisions.
items.why: Religious texts and social systems interact in ways that resist clean separation. The caste case shows how a tradition can be deployed for social hierarchy and also generate its own critics.

items.title: The earliest Christians thought Jesus would return within their lifetime
items.claim: Paul's letters (50s CE) are the oldest Christian texts. What does he tell his churches about the timing of Christ's return?

options.text: He explicitly warns that it will be many centuries away
He tells believers — in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 — that 'we who are alive, who are left' will be caught up to meet the Lord
He refuses to discuss the timing at all
He places the return precisely at AD 70, the destruction of the Temple

items.reveal:
1 Thessalonians 4:15-17, written around 50-51 CE, includes Paul among those still alive at the Parousia. 1 Corinthians 7:29 says 'the appointed time has grown short.' Mark 9:1 has Jesus saying 'some standing here will not taste death' before seeing the Kingdom.

When Christ did not return, later texts (e.g. 2 Peter 3:8 — 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years') reinterpret the delay. This shift is one of the central transformations of early Christian theology.
items.why: Treating the New Testament as a unified, settled doctrine misses that it documents a community reinterpreting itself in real time. The 'delay of the Parousia' is one of the formative pressures on Christian thought.
